title: How to get value from AI tools you already pay for | Traq Collective
metaDescription: Most AI subscriptions go unused within months. Here is how to check who is actually using yours, fix the team where it stalled, and decide when to cancel.
targetQuery: how to get value from AI tools we already pay for
h1: How to get value from AI tools you already pay for
author: Nazir Dogan
intro: Getting value from AI tools you already pay for starts with checking who is actually using them, not buying anything new. Pull the usage report your subscription already gives you, find the one team or task where activation is lowest, fix that specific gap with a short hands-on push, and only then decide whether the licence is worth renewing.

bodySections.h2: What does it mean to get value from a tool you already pay for?
bodySections.body: This is a different problem from starting AI adoption from zero. The licence is bought, someone probably ran a demo or a training day, and the invoice keeps arriving whether anyone opens the tool or not. Value here is not a feature list or a seat count. It is whether a specific, named task now takes less time or produces something better because the tool is there. If nobody can point to one task that changed, the subscription is not delivering value yet, regardless of how many people technically have access to it.

bodySections.h2: How do you find out what's actually being used right now?
bodySections.body: Before fixing anything, look at the number. Every major AI subscription ships a usage report that most owners never open: Microsoft 365's admin center has a Copilot usage report broken down by user and app, ChatGPT Business and Enterprise workspaces have a built-in analytics dashboard showing active users over the last 30 and 90 days, and Google Workspace's admin console reports Gemini activity the same way. Pull the last 30 days and sort by team, not by company total. A company-wide average of 40% active use can hide one team at 90% and three teams at near zero, and it is the near-zero teams that tell you where to spend the next hour.

bodySections.h2: Why do AI subscriptions go unused even after a rollout?
bodySections.body: The typical company has already put an AI tool in most employees' hands, but only a quarter of them open it regularly: 85% of employees have access to at least one AI tool at work, yet only about 25% use it regularly, according to IBM's 2026 Global CEO Study, a roughly 60-point gap between being given a licence and actually opening it. Ask the people not using it why, and the honest answer is rarely fear of the technology. Among employees who have AI available but do not use it, 46% of non-users and 36% of infrequent users say they simply find their current way of doing the work easier, according to a February 2026 Gallup survey of over 23,000 US employees. The tool did not fail a technical test. It lost to the habit that was already faster for that person on that task.

bodySections.h2: How do you fix a stalled tool without re-running the whole rollout?
bodySections.body: Do not re-launch the tool company-wide again. Go back to the one team or task the usage report flagged and run a second, narrower push there. Book a hands-on session on that team's own files, not a generic demo, and give people something to finish by the end of it rather than something to watch. Comfort using AI nearly doubles after a structured, hands-on session on real work, from 43% to 72%, according to Slack's research on AI microlearning, which is why a second, more specific push usually beats writing the tool off after one quiet rollout. Name one person on that team as the point of contact for follow-up questions for the next month. A single name people can actually message closes more gaps than an FAQ page nobody reads.

bodySections.h2: When should you actually cancel the subscription instead of fixing it?
bodySections.body: Give the fix a real, time-boxed test: one hands-on session, one assigned task, thirty days. Then pull the usage report again for that same team. If activation moved and someone can name a task the tool now handles, it earned its renewal for that team, and you repeat the same audit on the next lowest-activation group. If usage is still near zero after an honest second push, the tool is a mismatch for that team's work, not a training problem, and it is cheaper to cancel that seat and either try the tool with a different team or stop paying for it entirely than to keep renewing a licence on hope.

faqs.q: We already ran a training session, why is usage still low?
faqs.a: One session rarely survives a busy week. People leave with a demo they watched, not a task they finished, and the habit never forms. Go back to the specific team with the lowest usage, run a second hands-on session on their actual files, and give them one task to complete with the tool before the session ends.

faqs.q: How do we check who is actually using an AI tool we pay for?
faqs.a: Open the subscription's own admin console. Microsoft 365 has a Copilot usage report, ChatGPT Business and Enterprise have a workspace analytics dashboard, and Google Workspace reports Gemini activity the same way. Pull the last 30 days and sort by team so a strong company average cannot hide a team that never opened the tool.

faqs.q: Should we cancel a tool if only a few people use it?
faqs.a: Not immediately. Give it one honest, time-boxed push first: a hands-on session on real work for the lowest-activation team, plus a named point of contact, then recheck the usage report in 30 days. Cancel based on that new number, not on the first quiet month.
